newsitem.title: USA: Corn prices drop on rain forecast, gasoline up.
newsitem.headline: Corn prices drop on rain forecast, gasoline up.

text.p: Corn prices fell on Wednesday as forecasts for rain in the Midwest eased fears that recent hot, dry weather would hurt the crop as it enters a key stage of growth this month.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for post-harvest delivery in December closed down 5-3/4 cents a bushel at $2.50-3/4. July corn fell 4-1/4 cents to close at $2.66-1/2.

Meteorologists on Wednesday said two rain systems were forecast to move across the Midwest between now and early next week, with the second system offering the best chance of rain for dry areas in central Illinois, a leading corn state.
The U.S. corn crop is in the early days of pollination, which is the key reproductive stage of development.
Extreme heat and dry weather during pollination interferes with the formation of corn kernels and cuts into corn yields.
"If it gets wetter we may go down further, and if it gets drier we may go up," said Smith Barney analyst Dale Gustafson. "If we don't know by Friday, Monday could be an interesting day again."

Soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November fell 16-3/4 cents a bushel to close at $6.09, but the nearby futures contracts dropped even further on talk that a large commercial grain firm may yet deliver cash soybeans against the July contract before it expires on July 22.
July soybeans fell 29 cents to close at $7.82.
"There were concerns of possible deliveries against the July," said Ann Frick, an oilseeds analyst with Prudential Securities.

Frick said a monthly report from the National Oilseed Processors Association on Wednesday also eased concerns about tight supplies at commercial crushers, which had driven soybean prices to 8-1/2 year highs above $9 a bushel in May.
Soybean processor stocks rose 4 million bushels to 139.9 million bushels in June, compared to 175 million at the same time a year ago.

In New York, silver futures fell sharply as speculators sold heavily after another government report indicated that inflation remains tame. September silver at the COMEX ended down 11.2 cents at $4.185 an ounce.

The consumer price index in the United States in June rose only 0.1 percent, while the seasonally adjusted annual rate of 2.4 pct during the first six months of 1997 was the lowest since a 1.2 percent rise in the first half of 1965.
"Silver in particular now looks like it's heading south for the summer," FIMAT Futures trader John Tyree said.

"September silver broke down out of the range of the past week, under pressure from selling by funds and locals at the close, but gold did not follow to the same extent as it had already been sold off heavily last week," he said.
August gold at COMEX ended down 30 cents at $318.70 an ounce.

"The market is still bearish on gold, as there's still little incentive for investors, given potential central bank and producer selling, and given that overall commodity markets still have an disinflationary tone," Paine Webber senior analyst Bernard Savaiko said.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline prices ended higher after weekly U.S. oil inventory data showed declining supplies of gasoline, especially the grade deliverable against the NYMEX contract.
August gasoline settled 0.52 cent a gallon higher at 60.46 cents. August crude ended down two cents at $19.65 a barrel and August heating oil down 0.27 cent a gallon at 52.68 cents.

The American Petroleum Institute said total gasoline stocks fell 3.5 million barrels in the week ended July 11, a slightly larger drop than traders expected. Stocks of reformulated gasoline, the grade deliverable against the NYMEX contract, declined by 1.9 million barrels.

Crude was pressured by statements from Western diplomats that once Iraq resumes oil exports under a deal with the United Nations, it will have to do so at a fast pace to make up for lost time in reaching its quarterly oil sales limit of $1 billion.
